Reformed Baptist
ree-FORMD BAP-tist
noun phrase (tradition)
"Reformed" denotes adherence to the Calvinistic doctrines of grace and the Reformed confessional tradition; "Baptist" denotes believer's baptism by immersion and congregational government. The compound names the modern movement that recovers the 17th-century Particular Baptist heritage and the 1689 Confession.

📖 Biblical Definition

"Reformed Baptist" names the modern confessional movement that holds the full Reformed (Calvinistic) doctrines of grace together with believer's baptism by immersion, congregational church government, and (typically) subscription to the 1689 Second London Baptist Confession of Faith. The Reformed Baptist is, in doctrine, a Particular Baptist: he affirms the five points of Calvinism (total depravity, unconditional election, definite atonement, effectual calling, perseverance of the saints), the regulative principle of worship, the covenant theology of the 1689 (with its distinctive Baptist refinement of the relationship between the old and new covenants), and the plurality of elders in the local church. The modern movement traces to the mid-20th-century recovery of Reformed theology among Baptists — spurred by the Banner of Truth Trust's reprinting of the Puritans, the influence of figures like Ernest Reisinger and Walter Chantry, and the founding of confessional Reformed Baptist associations (ARBCA in America; the broader 1689-confessional networks). It distinguishes itself both from broad evangelical Baptists (who are often Arminian or non-confessional) and from Presbyterians (with whom it shares Reformed soteriology but differs on baptism, church government, and the relationship of the covenants). The Reformed Baptist tradition is the doctrinal home of U.S.M.C. Ministries' confessional commitments: the dictionary's voice-lock names the 1689 as its primary subordinate standard precisely because it stands in this tradition.

REFORMED BAPTIST, noun phrase. Reformed (Calvinistic) doctrine + believer's baptism + congregational government + (typically) 1689 subscription.

In doctrine a Particular Baptist: five points of Calvinism, regulative principle, 1689 covenant theology, plurality of elders.

Modern recovery spurred by the Banner of Truth Puritan reprints and figures like Ernest Reisinger and Walter Chantry; confessional associations such as ARBCA.

Distinguished from broad-evangelical Baptists (often Arminian/non-confessional) and from Presbyterians (different on baptism, polity, and the covenants).

The doctrinal home of U.S.M.C. Ministries' confessional commitments; the 1689 is the dictionary's primary subordinate standard.

📖 Key Scripture

Acts 8:36-38 — "And as they went on their way, they came unto a certain water: and the eunuch said, See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?... And they went down both into the water, both Philip and the eunuch; and he baptized him."

Ephesians 2:8-9 — "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."

Titus 1:5 — "For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee."

Jeremiah 31:33-34 — "But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts... for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them, saith the LORD."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Reformed Baptist identity is corrupted when "Reformed" is reduced to the five points alone (stripped of the confession, the regulative principle, and covenant theology), when it is treated as a fashionable brand rather than a confessional commitment, or when the "young, restless, Reformed" enthusiasm is mistaken for the settled confessionalism the name properly denotes.

expand to see more

Five-points-only reduction. In the early 21st-century "young, restless, Reformed" resurgence, "Reformed" was widely reduced to mean simply Calvinistic soteriology — the five points and nothing more. A genuinely Reformed Baptist identity is broader and deeper: it includes the whole 1689 Confession, the regulative principle of worship, a developed covenant theology, the plurality-of-elders church government, and a sacramental (ordinance) theology. A man who holds the five points while rejecting the confession, embracing pragmatic worship, and operating with a thin ecclesiology is a Calvinistic Baptist but not yet a confessionally Reformed one. The name properly denotes the whole confessional package, not the soteriology alone.

Brand-over-confession misreading. The Reformed resurgence produced a marketable "Reformed" brand — conference culture, celebrity preachers, a recognizable aesthetic — that can be adopted without the underlying confessional substance. A church may signal Reformed identity through its music, its book table, and its conference attendance while remaining doctrinally and ecclesiologically thin. The Reformed Baptist tradition is constituted by confessional subscription and the settled life of the local church under its elders, not by participation in a movement's culture. The 1689 is a confession to be subscribed and lived, not a brand to be worn.
